How do people combat this? Do the attackers eventually just give up?

Usually they give up or eventually as said in the video everyone stops listening/directing traffic from those servers or those protocols. It's been a long time since I was in classes for networking so I could be off.

How do people combat this?

Usually by having a lot of extra capacity. Either themselves (Google, Amazon, etc.) or hiring someone else to do it for you (Cloudflare, etc.). Also, noticing things that the attackers have in common that real users don't and taking advantage of those things to filter out the attacker's traffic.

Do the attackers eventually just give up?

Yes. Most DDoS attacks are done by botnets for hire these days. So, people literally pay by the hour for a DDoS of a given magnitude. OTOH, DDoS attacks by people who run their own botnets usually last until the attacker gets bored. If the attack is having no noticable effect, they usually get bored pretty quickly. Especially because the bots are much more likely to get cleaned up for being "slow" when they're part of an active attack.

I loved this game as a kid, but I also recognized it was utter crap. I later learned that most of the intro library for the NES was what we would consider shovelware today. To put it in perspective, the first games my family got were this and Athena. Both utter crap, but this one at least held my pre-teen focus for a few minutes at a time.

The controls were much worse than this video states, and you saw a bit of the character going invisible when shot, one thing that might not be apparent was that all your momentum stopped as well. If you didn't go invisible you got knocked back when shot. This led to frustrating and/or hilarious consequence, depending on if you were the one playing at the time.

The game had two phases, in general a two-part side-scrolling platform level, followed by a side-scrolling shooter level with a boss. The shooter bits were a lot more fun, and a lot more frustrating, than the bits shown in this video. The guy playing in this video clearly failed at walking forward in a straight line with a couple jumps, which is almost all that's required to make it to the end of this first bit.

The video also touched on the overall meh-ness of the game. Everything about it was average, except the stuff that was broken, which made it close to unplayable. Despite that I liked the look of it, and it was a challenge to avoid some of the glitchiness, giving certain levels an artificial difficulty much higher than they initially looked. With as clunky as this game is, I bet there are some truly exploitable glitches, but I doubt it would be worth looking for them, which is a shame in and of itself.

In conclusion, this was a bit of nostalgia for me. If suddenly there was a NES with this game in front of me, I'd probably say that's awesome, and then continue browsing Voat.
